title: Order, degree — or no degree at all
intro: Classify each equation by its degree. Read carefully: one bucket exists because the question sometimes has no answer.

buckets.label: Degree 1
buckets.hint: Highest derivative appears to the first power

buckets.label: Degree 2 or more
buckets.hint: Highest derivative raised to a power

cards.text: y″ + (y′)² = x — the highest derivative is y″, and it appears linearly
dy/dx = -2xy, the separable equation behind the Gaussian family

debrief:
The card doing the real teaching is `y″ + (y′)² = x`. It is tempting to call it degree 2 because there is a square in plain sight — but degree refers to the power of the **highest** derivative, which here is y″, and y″ appears linearly. Degree 1. The squared y′ is a lower-order term and does not enter the definition.

The undefined bucket is not a dodge. When a derivative sits inside cos, e^x or sin, the equation is not polynomial in its derivatives and degree is **not defined** — not zero, not one, not 'effectively one'. This matters beyond pedantry: order and degree are how you decide which solution method even applies, and a classifier that invents a number there sends you down a method that cannot work. Returning 'undefined' is the informative answer, in the same way that a blank field means 'nobody looked' rather than 'no'.

Note too that order is untroubled by all of this. Every card above has a perfectly well-defined order — it is only degree that can fail to exist.
